report:
# Does Magnesium Improve Depression Symptoms? A Look at the Evidence

**Short answer: Likely yes, but the evidence is preliminary and mixed rather than conclusive.**

## What the research shows

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) found that magnesium supplementation significantly reduced depression scores in adults with depressive disorder, with a large effect size (SMD: −0.919, 95% CI: −1.443 to −0.396) ([Frontiers in Psychiatry](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1333261/full); [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/)). However, the authors explicitly note that prior RCT findings on this topic have been **inconsistent**, which is why the meta-analysis was undertaken in the first place.

A separate systematic review and meta-analysis published in *BJPsych Open* examined magnesium and mood disorders more broadly, including both dietary intake and supplementation studies. It found that magnesium-rich diets were associated with lower depression risk in cross-sectional studies, but this association did **not hold up in prospective (longitudinal) studies** ([Cambridge/BJPsych Open](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open/article/magnesium-and-mood-disorders-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/9257DB9E4EAC7F0A5C5B84E63B4D3AEF)) — suggesting caution about causal claims.

A frequently cited individual trial (Tarleton et al., 2017, *PLoS One*) tested 248 mg/day of elemental magnesium in adults with mild-to-moderate depression and reported improved depressive symptoms within two weeks.

## Caveats

- Trial sizes are generally small, and effects appear strongest in people with low baseline magnesium or existing depressive symptoms rather than the general population.
- Cross-sectional dietary associations don't consistently replicate in longitudinal designs, raising questions about reverse causation or confounding.

## Conclusion

The evidence leans toward "yes," particularly for people with mild-to-moderate depression or magnesium deficiency, but the research base is still limited, inconsistent across study designs, and needs larger, more rigorous trials before magnesium can be considered a proven depression treatment.
